title: I Used the Batting-Cage Token Clock on the Coach Who Fed His Own Hopper

parts.text: I bought twenty pitches at 6:18 p.m. and coach Hal was already feeding the hopper from a staff sleeve while my token blinked READY. The window said: TOKENS FIRST. STAFF SLEEVES AFTER PUBLIC. I was fifteen's dad, holding a receipt. Hal kept feeding. "Coaches are the machine." I photographed the READY token, the sleeve, and the window. Then I logged a feed. At 6:25 the cage manager asked why Hal's sleeve was on a paid READY. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The cage manager can see Hal's staff sleeve feeding during a paid READY token.

social.description: Batting cage, a READY token, and a staff sleeve. I logged the feed. Would you have photographed the hopper?

parts.text: Hal called it a jam until the manager asked for the log. I printed the feed, the photo, and the window. The sleeve stopped. Hal jammed after public and told parents jams were always about optics. Optics is a word coaches use when a sleeve exists. Token policy now has a second line: COACHES ARE NOT THE MACHINE. I keep twenty. Hal waits. The cage finally throws a token, not a title. I kept the printout in a folder labeled BORING. I have learned the difference between a title and a line item.
